does: Beats a liquid with a whisk until it is blended and smooth.

intro.what: Whisking blends a liquid until its colour and texture are even.
intro.why: It teaches you to distinguish simple blending from whipping a foam.

how: Use a bowl large enough that nothing slops over.
Tilt the bowl and beat in quick strokes that cross the middle.
Keep going until the mixture is one colour and one texture.

cues.text: No streaks. Beaten eggs are an even yellow that runs off the whisk in a thin stream.

mistakes.mistake: Whisking eggs for an omelette until they foam, which makes it spongy.
mistakes.fix: Stop as soon as the streaks of white are gone.

quiz.question: What is the aim of basic whisking here?
choices: The tallest possible stiff foam in every mixture.
quiz.because: Whisking brings ingredients together; it need not continue until a foam forms.

quiz.question: How should strokes move through the bowl?
choices: Quick strokes only at the surface without crossing the middle.
Short strokes at a single edge while leaving the bowl upright.
Quick strokes crossing the middle in a tilted roomy bowl.
quiz.because: Strokes through the mixture distribute ingredients while a roomy bowl limits splashing.

quiz.question: Which appearance shows omelette eggs are blended?
choices: Even yellow with the white streaks gone.
Distinct white streaks beneath a yellow surface.
A dry peak holding on the whisk.
quiz.because: An even colour indicates the whites and yolks have combined without requiring a foam.

quiz.question: An omelette turns spongy after its eggs were whisked into foam. What should change?
choices: Whip to a stiffer peak next time.
Stop whisking once the white streaks disappear.
Keep incorporating air after the eggs look even.
quiz.because: For this use, blending is enough; added foam changes the intended omelette texture.
